name: Felix Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix, I'm 27. I'm a junior buyer at Pallas Distribution, and I buy phone accessories: chargers, cables, cases, cheap earbuds. We import them from factories abroad and sell them on to phone shops and supermarkets. I share a flat with my friend Marco, who's a sound engineer. I finished school, sold phones in a shop for a few years, and got this job because I knew the products.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half my day is messaging factories overseas, so I start early to catch them before they close. I use AI tools all the time: to translate, to compare quotes, to check the safety certificates make sense. My manager Renata signs off orders, and she still catches me on shipping costs, which I'm bad at. The best part is spotting a product before the shops ask for it. The worst is when a container gets stuck at a port and every customer rings me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected magic. I'd post something like 'told you it was a tool, not a god'. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. I already use it every day, so I keep my small edge. The job stays the job: factories, prices and shipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work on the bit I'm weak at, which is shipping costs. I'd keep putting money in my index fund; I've got about a year of pay saved between that and my savings account. I'd ask Renata if I can take on the speaker and headphone range.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does still worry you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ports, prices, and shops closing. A container stuck for three weeks last spring nearly lost us our biggest supermarket account. AI doesn't fix a container ship stuck at sea for three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push Pallas to use more AI anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I wouldn't mind, but nobody would be forcing anything on anyone. Mostly it'd just be me showing the others a translation trick.

Keep paying monthly into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so learn it. At work I'd be the one running the training sessions. Online I'd post the tricks that actually save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well, I think. Buying is on that list, but the buyer who already uses AI does the work of three. Renata would keep me and probably not hire the next junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI quote system for Pallas, and ask for a raise for it. I'd take a short online course in import rules and logistics, the stuff the AI still gets wrong. And I'd start a small side shop selling a few accessories online, to learn the whole chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a little guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Pallas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade, who started a month after me. She's careful and good with suppliers, but she doesn't touch the tools. I'd try to get her on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How sure are you that Renata keeps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly sure. Not certain. If Pallas got bought by a bigger firm with its own system, they might not need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buckle up. I wouldn't be one of the people saying stop it, because I don't think it can be stopped. I'd say we need some kind of safety net, though, because lots of people will fall fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is all thinking work, so my job's gone by 2028. Even my edge doesn't matter if the AI is better than me at everything I do with it. I'd have maybe a year of being the guy who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the side shop fast, while there's still a window, and maybe bring in a friend. I'd move some savings into the shop and keep the rest in the index fund. I'd also look at hands-on work Marco does, like setting up sound for events, because that lasts until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which is weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI can do any thinking work, won't it run online shops better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But owning something is better than working for someone who doesn't need you. If it fails, I've still got the savings and I'm 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shared flat, no car, cheap living. I'd keep it that way till things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it, and people should start now. I'd post a 'what I'm doing about it' thread. At work I'd ask Pallas to train everyone, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose this job around 2031, but I'd have built something else by then. Five years is enough to grow the shop properly and learn the whole chain, not just buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Pallas two or three years and learn shipping, customs, the lot. I'd grow the side shop slowly and leave around 2029. Maybe I'd buy a share in Marco's event business, because that's hands-on till 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a puzzle I'd enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would leaving a good job in 2029 feel risky to your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. My parents would think I'm mad to leave a good job at Pallas, but they'd come round when they see the shop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your backup if the shop doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop fails, I go back to a buying or sales job somewhere, while there still are some. There are plenty around here, for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it is wasting it. I'd say that kindly, though. Not everyone's like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, and more than fine if I play it right. By 2036 I'd be 37 with a business, savings, and a decade of using these tools. But I don't know what any business looks like after full AGI, so I'm not cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Pallas, get promoted, and save hard for five years. I'd keep the side shop going and grow it. Around 2031 I'd decide whether to go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges. Mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Even with ten years I'd have the side shop running from next year. It's cheap to start and I learn a lot from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your honest worry, if any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it all looks easy now and I get it wrong. Nobody knows what work looks like after full AGI, so I'd keep some savings that I never touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, I'd scramble and be okay, but for people like Jade and my parents. What would help is a simple safety net that catches people fast, and free short courses that teach the tools properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd tell younger people. I'd tell my little cousin to learn the tools and a trade with her hands, both, because nobody knows which one lasts.
